newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland bombs deal new blow to peace process.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland bombs deal new blow to peace process.

text.p: Car bombs at the British army's Northern Ireland nerve centre on Monday ended a two-year moratorium by rival guerrillas on attacks in the province and dealt a huge blow to attempts to reach a political settlement.

The explosions, believed to have been carried out by the IRA or a radical offshoot which shares its goal of a united Ireland, raised the prospect of a return to the grim cycle of tit-for-tat sectarian violence the province knew for 25 bloody years.

No group claimed responsibility for the attacks, the first on a British security target in Northern Ireland since the IRA and its Protestant Loyalist rivals called ceasefires in 1994 to get their political spokesmen to the negotiating table.

But politicians on both sides of the Protestant/Catholic divide united in suspecting the Irish Republican Army, an underground militia committed to forcing Britain to abandon the homeland it set up for Protestants seven decades ago.

"I am horrified....it would appear to be the work of a republican paramilitary grouping. I do not know whether it is the provisional IRA," said Joe Hendron, whose SDLP party is the moderate, legal face of Irish Republicanism.

The timing, method and audacity of the attack on the headquarters of Britain's 18,000-strong military force in Northern Ireland all pointed to the IRA or an ally trying to score key political points at a critical moment.

It was mounted as British Prime Minister John Major was preparing to address his ruling Conservative Party's annual conference. Major is accused by the IRA of wrecking the peace process by insisting that it lead to the disarming of the IRA.

The IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, has been excluded from limping Anglo-Irish peace talks under way in Belfast since June because of the guerrillas' decision to end their 17-month truce in February.

But the IRA confined its bombing attacks to the British mainland and an army base in Germany to try to force the London government to drop its insistence that the IRA disarm to earn its Sinn Fein political wing a seat at the talks.

The attack sent shivers through the Catholic 40 percent of Northern Ireland's population. "I daresay we shall hear the Loyalist response to this from the barrel of a Loyalist gun," said one Belfast resident.
Monday's car bomb attacks follow the discovery in London of a huge IRA bomb factory and similar discoveries in Ireland.
Traditionally, the IRA is never more dangerous than when it has suffered in the publicity war and mounts spectacular attacks to prove it is still a potent force.

The attack appeared timed to coincide with a debate among the IRA's Loyalist rivals about whether or not to abide by their two-year-old truce or go back to war against Catholic targets in Northern Ireland and Ireland itself.

The blast could be heard in the top-security Maze prison, where some of the jail's 500 Loyalist prisoners who were instrumental in calling the truce were debating whether or not to recommend maintaining it.
Loyalists, so-called because of their allegiance to the British sovereign, killed 900 Catholics to avenge IRA attacks before calling their truce.
Their ceasefire was rewarded by the inclusion in the peace talks of their political representatives, the Progressive Unionist Party and Ulster Democratic Party.
Gary McMichael of the UDP said: "This is the single most serious event in the peace process since its inception."

The talks have failed to make any headway and have been marred by in-fighting and attempts by the province's pro-British Unionist parties to ensure that if Sinn Fein ever reached the negotiations, the IRA would disarm first.
The IRA has ridiculed such thinking as "ludicrous" and is said by security sources to have enough weaponry to keep fighting well into the 21st century.
